concepts.title: A Scientist Reads Tennyson and Newton
concepts.definition: S. Chandrasekhar, the astrophysicist, opens with Tennyson's poem 'The Princess', whose song of the scholar gipsy contrasts the poet's grave matter-of-fact wisdom with the scientist's visionary search. He then turns to Newton's own letters -- the man of science confessing that he seemed like a boy playing on the seashore while the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before him.
concepts.key_idea: A poet's paradox and a physicist's seashore -- Chandrasekhar begins creativity where art and science meet.

solution_steps.explain: Tennyson contrasts the poet's matter-of-fact wisdom with the scientist's visionary hunger.
Newton's seashore image makes the greatest scientist a child before an undiscovered ocean of truth.
Creativity, Chandrasekhar suggests, is this shared humility and hunger across art and science.

concepts.title: Keats, Shakespeare and the Negative Capability of the Creative Mind
concepts.definition: Chandrasekhar quotes Keats's letter on negative capability -- the capacity to remain in uncertainties and mysteries without any irritable reaching after fact and reason -- and Shakespeare as its supreme example. Creative minds, in science and art alike, must hold contradictory ideas patiently instead of forcing premature answers.
concepts.key_idea: Comfort inside uncertainty -- negative capability, Keats's name for the creative mind's patience with mystery.

solution_steps.explain: Negative capability is the power to stay inside uncertainty and mystery without grabbing at quick certainty.
Keats marvels that Shakespeare so possessed this capability -- entering every mind without imposing his own.
Chandrasekhar shows great scientists similarly dwelling with mysteries until nature yields -- patience as method.

concepts.title: Motivation and the Scientist's Search for Beauty
concepts.definition: Chandrasekhar closes with the motivation of the scientist: not utility alone but the search for beauty and order in nature -- the same aesthetic drive that moves artists. Patterns of creativity emerge as a common human pattern: discipline, humility before facts, endurance of uncertainty, and delight in a beauty the world had not yet seen.
concepts.key_idea: Beauty is the scientist's motive too -- creativity as one human pattern shared by laboratory and studio.

solution_steps.explain: Beyond fame or use, the scientist seeks the beauty of nature's hidden order.
Discipline, patience with uncertainty and humility before fact sustain the search.
Art and science share the pattern: humility, endurance, and delight in discovered beauty.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain negative capability with reference to Keats's description of Shakespeare.

solution_template.explain: Keats names the capacity to rest in uncertainties and mysteries without irritable reaching after fact and reason.
Shakespeare could inhabit every character's mind without forcing them into his own certainties.
That openness -- not possession of answers -- is what Chandrasekhar finds at the root of creativity.

worked_examples.question_pattern: What does Newton's seashore image tell us about the creative scientist's self-image?

solution_template.explain: Newton pictures himself a boy playing with pebbles while the great ocean of truth lies undiscovered before him.
Even the century's greatest achiever claims to have touched only the shallows.
Humility before the unknown, Chandrasekhar shows, is itself a mark of the creative mind.
